opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question. When I first started, I was very focused on the algorithm side, on whether I could make a model a bit more accurate, publish a paper, and push a benchmark number. That's a natural place to begin, because it's how a lot of us are trained to think about machine learning research.

Over time, my sense of what matters shifted quite a bit. Working on things like XGBoost taught me that the impact of an idea depends heavily on whether people can actually use it. A method that's elegant on paper but hard to run doesn't change much. A system that's fast, reliable, and easy to pick up can change how thousands of people work. So I started to care much more about the full stack: the algorithm, the system, and how they fit together.

That led me toward machine learning systems and compilers, projects like TVM and later MLC. The question became less "Can I invent a new model?" and more "How do we make these models run everywhere, efficiently, on whatever hardware people have?" I find that kind of problem really exciting, because it's where research meets real-world use, and because the right abstractions can unlock a lot of things you didn't anticipate.

The other big change is how I think about open source and community. Early on I thought of research as something you do and then publish. Now I see building a community around a project as part of the research itself. When people use your work, report problems, and extend it in directions you never imagined, you learn things you could never learn alone.

So if I had to summarize: I went from optimizing for papers to optimizing for impact and usability. I'm still asking hard research questions, but I'm much more motivated by whether the answers end up in people's hands.

r001.rationale: The response says Chen shifted from optimizing for papers to optimizing for impact and usability, but it does not describe choosing problems according to his own research taste.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think it has changed quite a lot, actually.

When I first started, I was very much driven by the problem in front of me. I wanted to win a competition, or I wanted a model that would train faster on my own machine. XGBoost really came out of that kind of motivation. I had a specific need, the existing tools weren't good enough, so I built something. I wasn't thinking about it as "research" in the grand sense. I was thinking, how do I make this thing work, and work well.

Over time, I think two things shifted. The first is that I started to care much more about the system behind the model than the model itself. Working on MXNet, and then TVM, I realized that a lot of what limits progress in machine learning isn't a lack of ideas. It's that the ideas are expensive to try. If it takes you weeks to get a new operator running efficiently on a new piece of hardware, you simply won't explore that space. So my sense of what matters moved from "what's the best algorithm" toward "how do we remove the friction so that many people can find the best algorithm."

The second shift is about abstraction and leverage. Early on I was happy to hand-tune something for one case. Now I'm much more interested in the question of what is the right layer of abstraction so that you solve the problem once and it keeps paying off. Compilers are a natural place for that, because a compiler is really a bet that you can capture a class of optimizations rather than one optimization. That's a different taste than I had as a student.

And honestly, the thing I underestimated the most was the community side. I used to think of a research contribution as a paper or a piece of code. Now I think the contribution is often the ecosystem around it, the people who pick it up, extend it, and take it somewhere you didn't expect. XGBoost went places I never planned. TVM has gone places I never planned. So part of how I choose problems now is asking, if this works, can other people build on top of it without needing me in the loop?

So if I had to summarize, I went from wanting to solve the problem to wanting to build the tools that let many people solve many problems. And lately, with large models, that question feels more urgent than ever, because the gap between what the hardware can do and what people can actually deploy is still very wide.

r001.rationale: The response describes shifts toward systems, abstraction, and community when choosing problems, but it does not say his motivation shifted from publishing papers or that he now chooses problems guided by his own research taste.

astra-6.text:
I think my sense of what I want to work on has become less tied to a particular technique and more tied to a problem. When you first start doing research, it’s natural to ask, “What’s an interesting idea I can try?” Over time, the question becomes, “What’s something that really needs to work better, and what would it take to make that happen?”

That also changes how I think about the outcome. A paper can be a useful way to communicate an idea, but I’m increasingly interested in whether other people can build on it. Can it become a tool that helps someone do something they couldn’t do before? And when they use it, what do we learn about the next research problem?

So there’s still that curiosity about new ideas, but I think I’ve become more patient about following a problem through.

r001.rationale: The response says his focus has shifted from techniques and paper outcomes toward problems that need solving and work others can build on. It does not say those problem choices are guided by his own research taste.

sol-6.1.text:
I think, early on, I was more focused on a particular technical problem: can I come up with a better algorithm, or make a system faster? The problem itself was exciting, and solving it felt like the goal.

Over time, I’ve become more interested in what solving that problem enables. Who can use the result? Does it make something easier for other people to build? And is there a broader set of problems that becomes accessible because we built the right tool?

So I still enjoy going very deep technically, but I spend more time questioning the direction. You can do a lot of good work on a problem and then realize that the assumption behind it has changed. I want to stay open to that—to let what we learn change the research question, rather than becoming too attached to the question we started with.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from solving technical problems toward considering what the work enables and rethinking research direction. It does not describe a shift away from publishing papers or say that problem choice is guided by his own research taste.
